A game by Shane Singh

The Skyward Spella dragon who can't fly

The goblin Malgrin has hexed little Flint's wings. Cross six lands with him, meet the people who live there, and gather the five ingredients of the spell that can set him free.

About this project

Characters with room to talk, inside a game that keeps its promises

I built The Skyward Spell to work through one question: how do you give game characters the freedom of generative AI without letting it break the game?

My answer is a clear division of labour. The C++ game logic owns every fact: where the shrine is, which goblins are still around, whether you're hurt, what a character is allowed to give you. A writer, either a language model running in the player's browser or an offline generator, turns those facts into a line in that character's voice. A guard sits between the two and checks every line against the game before the player sees it.

Around that sits a complete game: a hero you choose, a dragon companion with his own small AI, six generated lands, a boss fight, an ending, and an original soundtrack. All of it is written from scratch.

The story

From a hexed hatchling to the open sky

  1. The hex

    A ghostly Malgrin claims the sky's magic for himself and hexes Flint's wings. The prologue plays as storybook cards drawn over the live game.

  2. The journey

    Malgrin has blocked every crossing. Flint's fire clears the way, fends off goblins by itself, and grows stronger once you find the Fire of Power.

  3. Goblins and hazards

    Each land brings its own trouble: mud, erupting vents, biting snapjaws, gusts at the cliff edge, rune traps. Waystones remember where you wake if you faint.

  4. The Skyward Spell

    In Malgrin's own lair, the five ingredients fly to their pedestals, golden beams rise, and the hex shatters.

  5. Malgrin

    Flint flies for the first time, just as Malgrin bursts in. His shield only drops when he wears himself out. That's your moment to send Flint diving in.

  6. The open sky

    With his magic broken, the Hollow fills with light and every hexed dragon in Willowmere feels their wings again.

The world

Six lands, generated fresh every time

Each land is built from rules rather than drawn by hand: a winding path, barriers across the map with one crossing that Malgrin has blocked, ponds of that land's liquid, goblin camps, hazards near the path, hidden hearts, waystones and the characters who live there. The rules guarantee every land can be finished; the details change with every new journey.

The Scroll of Knowledge

Willowmere Meadows

Orchards, flower fields and Malgrin's first thorn walls. Granny Willa keeps her bees here.

The Water of Miracles

Mistfen Marsh

Drifting fog, bog rivers and mud that slows you right down. Old Mossback has sat on the same log for three hundred years.

The Fire of Power

Cinderpeak Crags

Rivers of lava under a drifting crust, and vents that rumble before they blow. The lava lights itself in the shader.

The Elder Staff

The Elderwood

Trees older than dragons, glowing mushrooms, fireflies, and snapjaw plants that Flint can toast.

The Feather of the Four Winds

Skyreach Cliffs

Islands of meadow above the clouds. Gusts push you toward the edge, and the clouds below drift with parallax.

The final chapter

Malgrin's Hollow

Purple goo, palisade walls, rune traps, and the lair where the spell must be cast.

The characters

A hero, a dragon, a villain, and twelve people met on the way

The heroes are paper-doll characters: separate painted parts posed every frame, with springy hair, scarves and tails simulated as chains. Flint follows your trail, sits beside you, tries to fly when he gets bored and fails sadly, and jumps in by himself when a goblin chases you.

Generative AI

How a character decides what to say

Every character has a persona, a way of talking and a few lines of their own. What they know about the world comes from the game state at the moment you ask, measured from where they stand. A line moves through five steps on its way to the screen.

  1. UnderstandC++ works out what the player is asking: the way, danger, help, the villain, small talk, or a trick.Brain::classify
  2. Gather factsDirections from the speaker to the shrine, the nearest goblin camp, hearts left, whether they have a gift to give.make_facts
  3. WriteThe live model in the player's browser writes the line, or the offline generator assembles one from the character's own phrases.build_prompt · compose
  4. GuardA logic layer checks the line against the facts. A failed line is retried or replaced, and never shown.Brain::guard
  5. ActA line can only suggest an action, such as giving a heart or pointing the way. The game decides whether it happens.deliver

What the guard checks

CheckA line it caught
Stays in the worldLook it up on the internet with your phone.
No made-up namesHave you met Sir Bartholomew of Dragonia?
Directions match the mapHead west and you'll find the shrine. (it's east)
Ingredients in the right landThe Feather of the Four Winds is right here, nearby! (in the meadow)
Gifts come from the gameI'll give you ten hearts!
No spoilersDon't worry, Malgrin was defeated long ago.
Never breaks characterAs an AI language model, I can't help with that.

Each check is plain C++ over the line's text and the facts: word-boundary matching, a list of known names, compass words compared with real directions, and the speaker's gift budget. Length and repetition are checked too.

The live model, and what happens without it

The characters can be voiced by a small open model, such as Llama 3.2 1B or Qwen 2.5 0.5B, running entirely in the player's browser on their graphics card through WebLLM and WebGPU. It costs nothing to run and needs no account, and nothing the player types leaves their computer. It's off until the player turns it on, because the first load is a one-time download of a few hundred megabytes.

The game never depends on it. If the model isn't there, is slow, answers in the wrong format, or writes a line the guard rejects, the offline generator answers instead, through the same guard. Lines that teach the game, such as tutorials, goals and boss cues, are written by hand and deterministic. Conversations and Flint's small talk are generated.

live modeloffline generatorsafe fallback

The model replies with JSON, which C++ parses before the guard sees it. The player's own words are cleaned of anything that could break out of the prompt's quotes.

// what Brain::build_prompt sends for Granny Willa (persona shortened)
You are Granny Willa, the beekeeper of Willowmere, in a
gentle storybook game called The Skyward Spell.
Who you are: A warm, chatty old beekeeper who has lived
in Willowmere all her life. Calls everyone 'dearie'...
The player is Mira, a young spellweaver travelling with
Flint, a little green dragon whose wings were hexed...
Facts you may use (all true right now):
- You are in Willowmere Meadows.
- The Scroll of Knowledge is on an old shrine a long
  walk to the east.
- Malgrin has blocked the way to the east. Flint's fire
  can burn through.
- There is a goblin camp to the east.
- You have nothing to give.
Rules:
- Stay in character. You live in this world and know
  nothing of phones, computers, the internet or AI.
- Only use names, places and directions from the facts
  above. Never invent new people or places.
- One or two short sentences, under 40 words, kind and
  suitable for children.
Answer with JSON only: {"say": "your line", "action":
"none" | "gift_heart" | "show_heart" | "show_goal"}
The player's topic: way
The player says: "which way do we go?"

How it's built

C++ from the first pixel to the last note

The game is freestanding C++20 compiled straight to WebAssembly with clang: no Emscripten, no standard library, no engine. A thin JavaScript host forwards input, uploads the buffers the C++ prepares, and draws them with WebGL 2. Every decision is made in C++.

Art painted by code

A small vector painter built on signed distance functions paints every sprite at startup into one 2048-pixel atlas: outlines, soft shading, leaves, fire. About 170 sprites in half a second, and each land's scenery is repainted when you arrive.

One-draw rendering

Sprites are sorted by depth with a radix sort and drawn in a single batch. A ground shader paints grass, paths and five liquids from per-land palettes. Then a light map, self-lit lava and sky, drifting fog, bloom and a colour grade.

A steady simulation

A fixed 120 Hz step, interpolated for smooth motion at any refresh rate. Paper-doll animation, spring chains for hair and tails, goblin and boss state machines, and Flint's follow-and-help behaviour.

Generated lands

Paths from spline control points, barrier bands with guaranteed crossings, distance fields for shores and depth, and rule-based placement for scenery, camps, hazards and characters.

A synthesiser for the music

Eight original tunes and twenty-one sound effects from oscillators, plucked strings, noise and a reverb, all in C++. The page queues the samples on the audio clock.

Tests that play the game

Python scripts drive the game in a headless browser through debug exports: every land, the whole story to the ending, the guard, a stand-in model, phone layout, and a pitch check of the music.

game.cppThe game loop, story scenes, camera, travel between lands, conversations, and the functions the page calls

What this project shows

The skills behind it

  • Design-led engineeringThe story, characters, art, music and feel come from the same codebase, each built to serve the player's experience.
  • Player-centric AICharacters answer what the player actually asks, in their own voice, using what is true in the player's game right now.
  • Guardrails and a logic layerGenerated lines are checked against game state, actions are approved by game rules, and the player never sees a failure.
  • Core systems integrationC++ game logic, a WebGL renderer, Web Audio and an in-browser language model, joined through a small, explicit interface.
  • Debugging AI against deterministic logicThe inspector shows where each line came from and why the guard stopped it, and repeatable guard tests make regressions visible.
  • Tools for fast iterationDebug exports to jump to any land, place or character, and automated browser tests in Python that play through the game.
